article.headline: Memory, Not CPUs or Photonics, Is the AI Infrastructure Bottleneck
article.lede: Investors hunting for the next AI hardware winner have chased GPUs, networking chips, and custom silicon in turn. A post on X argues the real answer has been hiding in plain sight: memory — specifically the high-bandwidth stacks that sit beside each GPU — where demand is doubling annually while supply remains structurally constrained. Micron's decision to abandon its consumer-DRAM brand in late 2025 is the clearest market confirmation yet.
article.body:
An Intel (INTC) earnings headline crystallised a genuine shift: as AI workloads migrate from *training* — the computationally intensive process of building a model — toward *inference*, the act of running one, datacentres need proportionally more CPUs for orchestration and control-plane tasks. Intel's data-centre and AI revenue rose 22.4% year-on-year in Q1 2026, and executives described the CPU-to-GPU cluster ratio compressing from the training-era norm of roughly 1:8 toward 1:1 for agentic workloads. @bradsferguson's point is not that CPUs are irrelevant; it is that **22% revenue growth looks modest once you run the arithmetic on what is happening inside every server added to the cluster**.

Each GPU shipped to a *hyperscale* datacentre carries a fixed allotment of **HBM** — *high-bandwidth memory*, a stacked form of *DRAM* in which multiple memory dies are bonded directly onto the processor package, achieving far greater data throughput than conventional memory. GPU unit volumes are expanding at roughly a third per year in datacentre deployments; the memory each GPU requires is expanding at roughly half again on top of that. NVIDIA (NVDA) makes the progression concrete: the H100 shipped with 80 GB of HBM3; the H200 with 141 GB; the B200 with 192 GB; the B300 Ultra with 288 GB — a 50% step in a single generation. Compounded with growing unit volumes, that produces something close to a doubling of total HBM demand annually. TrendForce, a Taiwan-based market research firm, put HBM demand growth at 130% year-on-year in 2025, comfortably ahead of the back-of-envelope estimate in the post.

The clearest market signal came in December 2025, when Micron (MU) announced it would wind down its Crucial consumer-DRAM brand — a product line it had sold for 29 years. Sumit Sadana, Micron's chief business officer, was direct: "the AI-driven growth in the data centre has led to a surge in demand for memory and storage." The company's chief executive separately disclosed that Micron can currently satisfy only 50% to two-thirds of demand from several key customers. **The entire global HBM industry is sold out through at least the end of 2026.** Supply is concentrated among three players: SK Hynix (000660.KS), which commands roughly 62% share; Micron; and Samsung Electronics (005930.KS). A structural constraint amplifies the scarcity: each byte of HBM requires approximately three times the semiconductor wafer area of conventional DRAM, so capacity cannot respond quickly even when prices surge.

The valuation gap is striking. Micron's *forward price-to-earnings* ratio sits near 7x — roughly 79% below the semiconductor sector median of about 34x — while Intel trades at close to 99x forward earnings on its inference-driven CPU recovery. Samsung's memory division and SK Hynix are on track to generate operating margins that analysts project will rival or exceed those of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) by mid-2026, yet both Korean companies trade at single-digit multiples on their semiconductor businesses. The historical knock on DRAM is that overcapacity can erase margins within a year. The counter-argument is that HBM is structurally different: a short supplier list, multi-year design cycles, and a dominant buyer in NVIDIA that cannot easily switch. Memory pure-plays remain cheap relative to the chokepoint they control.

The post draws a pointed contrast with **photonics** — the use of light rather than electrons for high-speed data transmission inside datacenter racks. The sector's central near-term technology is *co-packaged optics* (CPO), which integrates optical transceivers directly onto a switch or AI chip package to cut the energy and latency costs of shuffling data between GPUs. The investment case received a dramatic endorsement in March 2026 when NVIDIA committed $4 billion combined to Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE). Lumentum now trades at roughly 44x forward earnings — six times Micron's multiple — on revenues that are only beginning to scale, with volume CPO deployment in production clusters remaining largely a 2027-and-beyond prospect. The technology is real; the timeline risk is the complaint. As a relative trade, memory offers a demonstrated supply shortfall, a confirmed bottleneck, and a substantially cheaper entry price.

concepts.definition: The phase of machine-learning development in which a model's parameters are iteratively adjusted against a large dataset. It is computationally intensive and GPU-heavy, typically requiring many GPUs per CPU in a cluster.

The act of running a trained AI model to generate outputs — answering questions, producing text, orchestrating agents. Inference workloads are growing rapidly and require more CPU involvement than training for control-plane and orchestration tasks, particularly in agentic applications.

A specialised form of DRAM where multiple memory chips are vertically stacked and bonded directly adjacent to a processor die using microscopic vertical interconnects. HBM delivers far higher data throughput than conventional memory but is expensive to manufacture and requires roughly three times the semiconductor wafer area per byte compared with standard DRAM.

Dynamic random-access memory — the dominant technology for volatile computer memory, used in everything from laptops to servers. In AI datacentres it appears both as conventional server RAM and as the base material for HBM. DRAM has historically been a boom-bust commodity, though HBM represents a structurally more constrained variant.

A warehouse-scale computing facility operated by one of a small number of dominant cloud and internet companies — Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and a few others. Hyperscalers buy hardware in volumes large enough to set industry supply priorities and, in the case of memory, have displaced consumer buyers as the marginal customer.

A valuation ratio dividing a company's current share price by its expected earnings per share over the next twelve months. A lower forward P/E generally means a stock is cheaper relative to anticipated profits. The semiconductor sector median sits around 34x; Micron's is near 7x, Intel's near 99x.

A technology that integrates optical transceivers — the components that send and receive data as pulses of light — directly onto the same package as a network switch or AI chip, rather than in a separate pluggable module. CPO reduces energy consumption and latency for AI cluster interconnects but remains in early production deployment as of 2026.

The use of light-based components — lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and optical fibres — to transmit data inside computing facilities. In AI infrastructure, photonics is positioned as a successor to copper-wire interconnects for linking GPUs at high speed and low power, particularly in co-packaged and rack-scale architectures.

article.fact_check: The specific unit-level growth figures cited — 22% for CPUs and 33% for GPUs shipped to datacentres — do not appear as named statistics in any public IDC, Gartner, or company earnings filing; they may derive from a paywalled sell-side or research report. The closest public match for the CPU figure is Intel's DCAI revenue growth of 22.4% in Q1 2026, but revenue and unit shipments diverge when prices are rising. GPU-server revenue growth ran far above 33% (IDC-sourced data showed 192% revenue growth for GPU-equipped servers in Q4 2024 alone), suggesting the 33% figure describes units, not revenue — but no public unit count confirms it precisely. Separately, Intel executives framed the CPU-to-GPU ratio converging toward 1:1 as the trajectory for agentic AI workloads specifically, not a current market reality; current inference clusters are running closer to 3-to-4 GPUs per CPU. Neither caveat undermines the central argument: HBM demand growth of 100%-plus is well-supported by TrendForce data, and Micron's supply constraints are confirmed by company filings.

ticker_intc.name: Intel Corporation
ticker_intc.blurb: Intel is the world's largest semiconductor company by revenue (historically) and the only major chip company that both designs and manufactures its own processors at scale. Its product portfolio spans PC and server CPUs (Core, Xeon), AI accelerators (Gaudi), FPGAs (Altera), and networking silicon. Intel's foundry ambition — Intel Foundry Services (IFS), renamed Intel Foundry — aims to manufacture chips for external customers on its 18A and 14A process nodes, positioning the company as a Western alternative to TSMC. After CEO Pat Gelsinger was replaced in late 2024, the company has undergone significant restructuring.
ticker_intc.recent: Intel reported Q1 2026 revenue of $13.6 billion, up from a depressed base, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.29 versus a near-zero consensus — the beat sent shares up 20%+ in after-hours trading. Data-centre revenue grew 22% YoY. Full-year 2026 EPS estimates of $0.48–$0.56 would represent ~101% growth from the 2025 base — a base-effect figure that reflects restructuring charges and near-zero profitability rather than a dramatic business inflection. Intel trades at ~62.1x forward earnings with a PEG of 0.61 given the distorted growth denominator.

sources.title: Intel Stock Rose 24% After Q1 2026 Earnings — TIKR

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

sources.title: Micron HBM4 in mass production for Nvidia Vera Rubin

ticker_000660-ks.name: SK hynix Inc.
ticker_000660-ks.blurb: SK hynix Inc. researches, develops, manufactures, and sells semiconductor devices, including DRAM, NAND flash, SSD, MCP, and CMM products. The company serves server, networking, mobile, PC, consumer, and automotive markets. It is one of the world's largest memory chipmakers, competing directly with Samsung Electronics and Micron Technology.
ticker_000660-ks.recent: In the past 30 days, SK hynix reported earnings on April 23, 2026, with revenue and net income surging on a memory price upcycle. The stock hit a 52-week high of 1,653,000 KRW, reflecting strong demand for AI-related memory chips. Morningstar raised its fair value estimate by 65% following the earnings report.

ticker_005930-ks.name: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
ticker_005930-ks.blurb: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. is a South Korean multinational electronics company and the world's largest manufacturer of memory chips, smartphones, and consumer electronics. It operates through four divisions: Device eXperience (DX), Device Solutions (DS), SDC, and Harman, covering products from smartphones and TVs to semiconductors and home appliances. As of 2026, it holds a dominant market position in memory and mobile devices, with a market cap exceeding 1,700 trillion KRW.
ticker_005930-ks.recent: In the past 30 days, Samsung Electronics reported strong quarterly earnings driven by blistering memory price hikes, leading to a 46% increase in fair value estimates. The stock hit a 52-week high of 277,000 KRW, reflecting a 390% year-over-year gain. Analysts have raised price targets amid robust demand for AI-related memory chips.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.

ticker_cohr.name: Coherent Corp.
ticker_cohr.blurb: Coherent Corp. (formerly II-VI Incorporated, rebranded after the 2022 acquisition of Lumentum rival Coherent) develops and manufactures engineered materials, optoelectronic components, and laser systems across three segments: Networking, Materials, and Lasers. Its Networking segment — the primary AI data-center play — supplies indium-phosphide chips, transceiver modules, and silicon-photonics sub-assemblies to hyperscalers and networking OEMs. With roughly $5.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, it is one of the largest vertically integrated photonics companies in the world.
ticker_cohr.recent: Coherent joined the S&P 500 in March 2026, the same month it announced general availability of the industry's first dual-laser QSFP28-DCO module — a compact form factor enabling 100G coherent transmission over a single fiber with up to 300 km reach. At OFC 2026 the company showcased an expanded InP portfolio including 400 mW CW lasers, 200G/400G photodiodes, and 800G/1.6T modulators. Fifteen analysts hold an average "Strong Buy" rating with a consensus 12-month price target near $278.

ticker_lite.name: Lumentum Holdings Inc.
ticker_lite.blurb: Lumentum makes the lasers, optical chips, and components that go into the high-speed transceivers wiring AI data centres together. Spun out of JDSU in 2015, it spent its first decade as a 3D-sensing and telecom-optics supplier of moderate growth. The AI-cluster build-out has remade it into one of the principal upstream beneficiaries of hyperscaler capex, alongside Coherent Corp.
ticker_lite.recent: Q1 fiscal-2026 set record revenue, with management citing AI-driven demand and an order book that runs into 2027. In March 2026 Nvidia announced a roughly $2 billion strategic investment paired with multi-year purchase commitments for co-packaged-optics components. The company joined the S&P 500 in March 2026; shares have surged on AI demand, leaving the stock at a forward P/E in the 60s, materially above peers.
